title: Polish Prepositions: Which Case Each One Takes
excerpt: Polish prepositions decide the case of the noun after them. Get the full list with cases, motion vs location pairs, w vs na, and practice.
metaDescription: Polish prepositions decide which case follows them. See a list of 23 prepositions with cases, motion vs location pairs, w vs na, z vs ze, and practice.
summary: Every Polish preposition governs a case, so learn each one together with the case it takes.
W, na, za, pod, nad, przed and między switch case: accusative for motion, locative or instrumental for position.
Z means 'from' with the genitive but 'with' with the instrumental, and places split into w-places (do / w) and na-places (na / na).
W and z become we and ze before some consonant clusters and before mnie / mną, as in we wtorek and ze mną.

factNotes: No statistics or dated facts used. Left out 'na / w Ukrainie' (usage currently debated). The na-countries listed (Węgry, Słowacja, Litwa) were checked on Wiktionary; 'na Łotwie' is standard usage but its table was not checked. The claim that clock times like 'za dziesięć dziewiąta' keep the nominative comes from the site's own daily-routine-time lesson. The 'we' rule is worded as 'usually before w/f + consonant' because Wiktionary and PWN describe it only as 'before (certain) consonant clusters'. Removed an unverifiable remark that sports commentators prefer 'przeciwko'. Post office photo: Pixabay tags identify it as Poczta Polska in Bielsko-Biała, and the facade sign reads 'POCZTA POLSKA'.
